content: The World Health Organization (WHO) established the Maternal and Perinatal Health Guideline Development Group (MPH-GDG), which includes experts and stakeholders from all six WHO regions. This group comprises professionals with expertise in critically appraising research evidence, implementing evidence-based recommendations, developing guidelines, and addressing clinical practices, policies, and programs related to maternal and perinatal health. Their expertise spans various thematic areas within maternal and perinatal health. From this pool, 14 external experts and stakeholders were invited to update the recommendations. These individuals were chosen for their diverse expertise in research, guideline development, gender equity, rights, clinical policies, and programs related to the prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The group reviewed evidence, interpreted findings, and reached unanimous consensus on the final recommendations. An Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) was convened to conduct or update systematic reviews, appraise evidence, and develop Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks. A systematic review on the topic, supported by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, was updated. The WHO Steering Group reviewed the updated protocol and collaborated with the Cochrane group to appraise evidence using the GRADE methodology. Representatives from the Cochrane group and a methodologist attended the GDG meeting to present evidence and address technical questions. Evidence from other domains of the GRADE EtD frameworks was derived from systematic qualitative reviews exploring women’s and healthcare providers’ perspectives on childbirth and PPH prevention interventions. A systematic review on the cost-effectiveness of intravenous (IV) versus intramuscular (IM) oxytocin was also included. External partners, including representatives from USAID, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), and the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), participated as observers. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO, were identified as potential implementers of the recommendations. An External Review Group (ERG) of six technical experts reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. The priority outcomes for this update were aligned with the 2012 WHO recommendations on PPH prevention and treatment. Evidence was gathered from various sources, including updated systematic reviews, and critically appraised using the GRADE approach. Certainty of evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The GDG formulated recommendations based on explicit consideration of evidence presented in the EtD frameworks. These frameworks included domains such as effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, with no opposition expressed. The WHO Steering Group prepared draft documents, which were reviewed and modified during the GDG meeting. Following the meeting, a full guideline document was drafted to reflect the deliberations and decisions. This document was reviewed and approved by the GDG and ERG before being finalized. The recommendation adopted by the GDG was that oxytocin (10 international units, administered intramuscularly or intravenously) is recommended for the prevention of PPH for all births. In cases where women giving birth vaginally already have IV access, slow IV administration of 10 IU oxytocin is preferred over IM administration. This context-specific recommendation was based on evidence showing that IV oxytocin reduces the risk of PPH, severe PPH, blood transfusion, and severe maternal morbidity, with no significant differences in adverse effects. However, routine IV oxytocin use may require additional resources, impact women’s comfort, and increase health inequities. The GDG emphasized that IV access should not be routinely established solely for administering oxytocin for PPH prevention.
